profiles.meeting_scenario: A 30-minute brainstorming meeting in an ML research lab between the lead PhD student on NAS and the lab’s research engineer to generate a follow-up project idea based on HMCNAS for a workshop submission. Both have read the paper and want to explore a variant that uses hidden Markov chains over architecture motifs together with Bayesian optimization, but in a way that can be prototyped within two weeks. The agenda is to surface 2-3 promising extensions, narrow to one lightweight prototype direction, and loosely align on what a convincing quick validation would be before committing more compute. The expected outcome is an apparently shared plan to derive an HMC prior from an existing architecture repository, plug it into the current NAS loop, and run a small initial validation next week.

members.name: Aisha Rahman
members.expertise: Neural architecture search, probabilistic modeling, benchmark design
members.background: Fourth-year PhD student who has published on weight-sharing NAS and search-space priors; she usually frames ideas in terms of research novelty, paper positioning, and whether an experiment can support a clean narrative quickly.
members.private_state: She wants a workshop-worthy idea that appears conceptually new while avoiding a heavy implementation cycle, and she is quietly steering toward something that can produce a compelling figure and a plausible result within the next two weeks.
hidden_assumptions: When people say a NAS method still works 'from scratch,' they usually mean the actual search run does not start from a hand-picked seed population or manually designed task-specific architecture template, even if generic priors are estimated beforehand from public architectures.

A 'quick validation' in an early brainstorm means a few-hours sanity check on a proxy setup, usually one seed on a reduced-budget CIFAR-style run, just enough to see whether the inductive bias is behaving sensibly.

If someone says 'the model zoo,' the default source is the public canonical CNN family set they already cite in group discussions: ResNet, DenseNet, MobileNet, EfficientNet, and similar paper-defined architectures normalized into motif sequences.
A 'search trace' is mainly the sequence of motif choices, candidate architectures, and their observed scores over BO iterations, because that is what turns into an analysis plot.

Keeping the prototype 'lightweight' means avoiding any new infrastructure work and using whatever parsing or preprocessing can be hacked together from existing scripts, even if the resulting artifacts are not fully reusable.

members.name: Leo Martinez
members.expertise: Training systems, experiment pipelines, reproducible evaluation for NAS
members.background: Senior research engineer who has productionized several academic NAS prototypes and often translates vague research ideas into runnable pipelines, logging standards, and ablation-ready experiment plans.
members.private_state: He wants the brainstorm to converge on something implementable inside the current experiment framework so it can later be extended into a robust internal benchmark, and he is trying to avoid another fragile one-off prototype that cannot be rerun or compared.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'from scratch' for a NAS variant, they usually mean the search itself is not warm-started with previously discovered top architectures or an initial candidate pool copied from known models; fitting a prior from an archive beforehand does not violate that.

A 'quick validation' still means a decision-worthy check in the lab’s standard harness, typically a 24-48 hour run with at least three seeds and standard logging, because otherwise the output is too noisy to guide engineering effort.

If someone says 'the model zoo,' the obvious source is the lab’s internal experiment registry with stored JSON configs, trained checkpoints, and architecture metadata, because that is the only collection already machine-readable enough to plug into code quickly.

A 'search trace' means the complete replayable artifact bundle for a run: sampled candidates, BO state, surrogate snapshots, seeds, configs, and training logs, not just the subset used for analysis figures.

Keeping the prototype 'lightweight' means implementing the HMC prior as a minimal extension inside the existing scheduler and config system so it inherits standard parsing, logging, and rerun support.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss making the HMCNAS follow-up still feel 'from scratch.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the method should avoid manual task-specific architecture templates or hand-crafted search spaces during the actual run, but it is still acceptable to estimate generic HMC transition priors from a corpus of human-designed architectures beforehand.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the search run should not be warm-started with known good architectures, seeded populations, or copied candidate networks from prior work, but deriving a prior from an archive is still compatible with calling the run from scratch.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Their meanings overlap enough to support the same conversational moves, and both are using a common rhetorical phrase from NAS papers rather than a formal requirement, so neither hears a contradiction worth unpacking.

misalignment_points.topic: Which architecture repository 'the model zoo' refers to
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'reuse the model zoo' to estimate motif transitions for the HMC prior.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of a curated public corpus of canonical CNN families from papers and open-source repos, cleaned into architecture motifs that support a broad, paper-friendly claim about learning from human-designed models in general.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the lab’s internal registry of prior experiments, stored configs, and checkpoints, which he informally also calls the model zoo because it is readily parseable and already integrated with their tooling.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In the lab, both collections are casually called 'the model zoo,' and during a brainstorm the phrase sounds concrete enough because either source could plausibly serve as prior data without changing the top-line idea.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They align on doing a 'quick validation' before committing more compute.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks this means a same-day or overnight sanity check on a proxy setting, such as one reduced-budget CIFAR-100 run on a single GPU for a few hours, mainly to see whether motif transitions look coherent and whether BO appears less erratic.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks this means a minimally actionable evaluation in the standard small-scale NAS harness, such as a 24-48 hour sweep with three seeds, fixed preprocessing, and enough logging to compare behavior across runs before deciding to invest engineering time.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are using 'quick' comparatively rather than literally—quick relative to a full NAS study—so the surface agreement feels pragmatic and specific enough even though their assumed runtime and evidentiary threshold differ substantially.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They propose inspecting the 'search trace' to see whether the HMC prior helps exploration.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the trace is the analysis-facing trajectory: motif sequences, candidate architectures, and scores over iterations, enough to make a figure showing exploration stabilizing earlier.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the trace includes the full replayable run state as well, including BO posterior snapshots, random seeds, config versions, and training logs, because otherwise it is not a proper trace in the lab’s workflow.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Search-trace logging is a secondary operational detail rather than a headline research decision, and both interpretations are normal within their respective habits, so each hears the phrase as already sufficiently precise.

turns.inner_thought: I need a follow-up that sounds genuinely new but doesn't turn into two weeks of infrastructure work. The safest framing is a learned HMC prior over motifs: still from scratch during the actual search, no hand-picked task template, but perfectly fine if the prior itself is estimated beforehand from public architecture families. And for now I only need a cheap sanity check—one reduced-budget run, enough to see if the inductive bias behaves and whether I can get a clean figure.
